exam: A 7‑year‑old with well‑controlled epilepsy on phenobarbital develops jaundice. What should you do? — Stop phenobarbital, check LFTs, consider switching to oxcarbazepine.
Why is phenobarbital preferred over carbamazepine in a child with hepatitis B? — Phenobarbital is less hepatotoxic and cheaper.
A child with recurrent seizures has a normal EEG. What is the next investigation? — Check for structural lesions with CT/MRI if available.
What is the main reason to avoid valproate in a pregnant adolescent? — Risk of neural tube defects.
A child with epilepsy develops a rash after starting phenytoin. What is the likely diagnosis? — SJS/TEN; discontinue phenytoin immediately.
ai.title: Antiepileptic Drugs in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) are chosen based on seizure type, age, organ function and local availability. In low‑resource settings, first‑line agents are often phenobarbital or phenytoin, with careful monitoring for toxicity and drug interactions.

sections.p: AEDs are drugs that reduce the frequency or severity of seizures by modulating neuronal excitability. Diagnosis of epilepsy requires at least two unprovoked seizures or one seizure plus a high risk of recurrence.

t.b: Detects epileptiform activity; abnormal interictal spikes suggest epilepsy

sections.p: Epilepsy is staged by seizure frequency and control. In children, the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) classification guides treatment intensity.

t.b: Quantifies frequency; >4 per month indicates uncontrolled epilepsy

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, common reversible causes include infections (malaria, meningitis), metabolic disturbances, and herbal toxins. Structural causes such as cerebral palsy or brain malformations are also frequent.

t.b: Rule out hypoglycaemia as seizure trigger; <2.5 mmol/L is dangerous

b: Focal onset: unilateral limb clonus, speech arrest
Generalised tonic‑clonic: stiffening, loss of consciousness
Febrile: brief, <1 min, no post‑ictal confusion
sections.p: Seizures may be focal (motor, sensory) or generalized (tonic‑clonic, absence). Febrile seizures are common in 6‑12 month olds and usually benign.
Investigations are tailored to available resources. Basic labs and imaging are essential to exclude treatable causes.

t.b: ALT >5× ULN signals need to avoid hepatotoxic AEDs
Phenytoin and carbamazepine are renally cleared; adjust in CKD
Identify structural lesions; CT may be available in district hospitals

b: Status epilepticus: >5 min or repeated seizures
sections.p: Severe or refractory seizures, status epilepticus, or drug toxicity require urgent care. Monitor for hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and skin reactions.

t.b: If ALT 3–5× ULN, consider dose reduction

b: Use benzodiazepines (diazepam) for acute seizure control
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then initiate AEDs. In low‑resource settings, phenobarbital and phenytoin are preferred for their low cost and availability.
Regular review of seizure control, drug levels (if available), and side effects. Educate caregivers on adherence and avoidance of triggers.

t.b: Adjust dose if levels low or high

sections.p: Febrile seizures are benign and do not require long‑term AEDs, unlike epilepsy. Status epilepticus mimics severe infection or metabolic crisis.

b: ALT may rise late in hepatotoxicity
sections.p: In low‑resource labs, false‑negative malaria tests may miss a precipitating infection. Normal liver enzymes may still mask early hepatotoxicity.
